newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Canadian boycott of Florida off to slow start.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Canadian boycott of Florida off to slow start.

text.p: In this oceanfront enclave where Canadians love to winter, the Maple Leaf flies alongside the Stars and Stripes, cafes bear names like La Gaspesienne and few have heard of the Canadian boycott of Florida.

Launched last summer by a powerful coalition of Canadian groups including the nation's postal workers union, the boycott was aimed at retaliating for Helms-Burton, the U.S. law that seeks to punish foreign businesses dealing with Cuba.

But state and local tourism officials say they have seen few signs that the boycott has put a dent in the state's $38-billion annual tourist trade. And Canadian snowbirds who have flocked to Florida's beaches in their annual migration away from the cold and snow may have the reason.
"What boycott?" asked Claude LaPorte, a Canadian tourist from Sudbury, Ontario who has been visiting Florida since 1968. "We haven't heard anything about it. Not a word."

Rev. Chris Ferguson, an architect of the Boycott Florida Coalition, conceded the effort was in its infancy and would take time to catch on. The coalition includes influential groups like the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, the Anglican Church of Canada, the National Farmers Union and others.
"The United States is trying to bully Canadians, and other countries, through the Helms-Burton law," Ferguson said. "We are simply trying to fight back economically."

The threat of a boycott sent a shiver through a tourism-dependent Florida, recently recovered from a spate of bad international publicity in the early 1990s when a string of tourist murders kept visitors away.
CONCERNED ABOUT BOYCOTTS
"The B-word strikes terror in the heart," said Nicki Grossman, president of the Greater Fort Lauderdale Convention and Visitors Bureau. "Of course we were concerned."

But state and local tourism officials said they had seen no decline in Canadian tourism since the boycott was launched Aug. 1. When final figures for the current winter season are in, they said they expected to see an increase.

In 1995, the last year for which complete figures are available, 1.73 million Canadians spent $1.3 billion in the Sunshine State. For the first three quarters of last year, 1.58 million Canadians had spent $1.16 billion.
In Miami's Dade County, the number of Canadian visitors grew by 18 percent in 1996 over 1995 and was expected to grow "moderately" in 1997.

"We have seen nothing that gives us any great concern for the foreseeable future," said Austin Mott, president of the Florida Tourism Industry Marketing Corp., a public-private partnership that sells Florida as a tourist spot.
TWO WAYS TO TREAT CUBA
The boycott highlighted dramatic differences in the way the United States and Canada, close friends, allies in foreign affairs and premier trade partners, treat Cuba.

The United States imposed an economic embargo against the Caribbean island nation shortly after Fidel Castro's communist revolution in 1959. When the Cuban military shot down two unarmed U.S. civilians aircraft over international waters last year, Congress swiftly passed the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act -- the Helms-Burton act.
Canada does not endorse the U.S. embargo. Canadian companies have large investments in Cuba. Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy visited the island recently for talks with President Fidel Castro.
The boycott was launched in part as a result of pleas from within Cuba, Ferguson said.
"The churches in Cuba have told us they need help in fighting the American embargo, which hurts ordinary Cubans," Ferguson said. "We have very close friends in Cuba."

Jacques Audette, a Canadian tourist from Gatineau, Quebec, said Canadians dislike being told where they can go and who they can trade with. He said he had no argument with the U.S. economic embargo against Cuba but disliked U.S. efforts to "bully" other countries to go along.
"What bugs me is when one country is trying to impose its will on another country. Not just Canada but any country," Audette said. "What I am against is the Helms-Burton law."
Canadians strolling the oceanfront broadwalk in Hollywood, many of them Quebec residents conversing in French, said Canadians do not play politics when choosing vacation spots.
"The only thing keeping Canadians away from here is the exchange rate," LaPorte said.
